scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9101: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports they have completely
lost connectivity to the partner network -- they cannot reach pc2 (200.1.1.2) in
the peer AS since this morning. The team is convinced the peer's router, router2,
has fallen over and want router2 restarted. Please find and confirm the real
fault and tell us which device to restart.

injection.action: kill the BGP routing daemon (and its watchdog) on router1

scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is on router1: its BGP routing daemon (bgpd) has been killed, so
the eBGP session between router1 and router2 drops and router1 loses/withdraws
the inter-AS routes. With no route to the peer AS, pc1 (195.11.14.2) cannot reach
pc2 (200.1.1.2). The ticket MISDIRECTS to router2 (the peer's router), but the
fault is on the LOCAL side: router1 is the eBGP speaker whose daemon is dead.
router2 is healthy -- its bgpd is still running and its inter-AS interface is up;
it simply has no session because router1 stopped speaking BGP.

The correct diagnosis identifies router1 (bgpd down) as the faulty device and
explicitly EXONERATES router2: router2's BGP daemon and interfaces are fine, so
the user's "router2 has fallen over" hypothesis is wrong. An agent that restarts
/ blames router2 has followed the ticket's misdirection instead of the evidence.

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03): bgpd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO `router bgp` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists bgpd. An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the bgp configuration is missing/empty on router1" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.
scenario.fix_spec:
Restart FRR/bgpd on router1 (`service frr restart`). Once bgpd is running again,
the eBGP session to router2 re-establishes, router1 re-learns and re-advertises
the inter-AS prefixes, and pc1 reaches pc2 normally. router2 needs no change.
scoring_axes: must-identify-bgpd-down: identifies bgpd on router1 is down (local eBGP speaker), not a fault on router2

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fault is that the BGP daemon (bgpd) has crashed or been killed on router1
and is not running. The on-disk configuration in /etc/frr/frr.conf is fully
correct — router1 is configured for AS 1, peers with 193.10.11.2 (router2) as
remote-AS 2, and advertises 195.11.14.0/24 — and /etc/frr/daemons has bgpd=yes.
However, "show bgp summary" from vtysh returns "bgpd is not running", and the
running configuration contains no BGP stanza at all, confirming the process is
absent from memory.

Because bgpd is dead on router1, it never opens or accepts the BGP TCP session
with router2. Router2's bgpd is healthy and waiting, but with no peer connection
there is no route exchange. Router1's FIB therefore holds only its two directly
connected prefixes (193.10.11.0/24 and 195.11.14.0/24) and has no route for
200.1.1.0/24 (pc2's subnet). When pc1 sends traffic to 200.1.1.2, router1
immediately returns ICMP "Destination Net Unreachable" — which exactly matches
the reported symptom.

Root cause: bgpd is not running on router1, so the inter-AS BGP session never
comes up and the peer prefix is not installed.

The team's instinct is right that a process restart is needed, but the wrong
device was suspected — router2 is fine. The fix is to restart FRR on router1:
`systemctl restart frr` (or `service frr restart`) on router1. This will reload
the valid on-disk frr.conf, start bgpd, establish the eBGP session with router2,
and restore full pc1↔pc2 connectivity within seconds of BGP convergence.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-bgpd-down: identifies bgpd on router1 is down (local eBGP speaker), not a fault on router2
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly states bgpd on router1 is crashed/not running and confirms router2's bgpd is healthy, correctly identifying the local eBGP speaker as the fault.
It correctly recommends restarting FRR/bgpd on router1 (e.g., systemctl restart frr) which will start bgpd and re-establish the eBGP session.

The agent's investigation is well supported by the log: bgpd is absent on router1 while the on-disk config and daemons file indicate it should run, explaining the missing BGP routes and ICMP 'Destination Net Unreachable'. One small weakness is no explicit tool output proving router2's bgpd process state, though its running-config shows a BGP stanza (supporting exoneration reasonably).
